My first winter back in the UK was psychologically challenging. Working alone on my next book didn’t feel as enjoyable in cold, grey London as it had abroad. The 10th anniversary of my father’s death was approaching and I felt a profound loneliness which, much like the cold, began to seep into my bones. item.title: The Democratic party is at a critical crossroad. Can it do the right thing? | Osita Nwanevu
item.description: Americans are at a real point of decision – not election day, but this heady, uncertain moment after Until 2026, the most important midterm year of the last quarter-century was very probably 2010. Barack Obama famously called the elections a “shellacking” for the Democratic party and he was right. Thanks to a sluggish economic recovery from the Great Recession and backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, Republicans took control of the House with a 63-seat gain – the largest House sweep since the 1940s – and won six seats in the Senate. But the 2010 midterms were significant well beyond those numbers. It was the first election shaped by the rise of the Tea Party and its blend of rightwing economic populism and xenophobia. Those aligned with the movement lost nearly twice the number of races they won, but the presence of an energized hard-right contingent among Republicans in Congress shaped legislative outcomes for the remainder of Obama’s term and beyond. I managed to wrestle my Toyota Corolla to a stop without crashing and sat there, heart pounding, as I wondered what to do next.
